item.title: 4 ways the midterm elections could turn out, with a month to go
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Democrats are heading into the last month of the midterm elections campaign with ambitions going deeper and deeper into red territory, while Republicans are grim about their hopes of holding on to either chamber of Congress. Historically, the opposition party almost always makes gains in the midterms, and President Donald Trump is less popular than ever. His support has weakened especially with independents in high-quality polls and among swing demographics that propelled his 2024 majority. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. Republicans have also tended to underperform when Trump isn’t on the ballot because more consistent voters have shifted toward the Democrats. More Democrats voted in this year’s primaries - a sign that they are also more likely to turn out now, with early and mail voting already underway in 43 states leading up to Election Day on Nov. 3. The Democrats’ lead in national and battleground polls has expanded since Labor Day. There are reasons to suspect polls could be overestimating Democrats’ strength, though surveys did not systematically favor Democrats in the last two midterms. Republicans’ main advantage is money. GOP campaigns and allies are outspending Democrats in almost all the most contested races, thanks in large part to more than $180 million that has been pumped in from Trump’s war chest since Labor Day. The outcome will define the remainder of Trump’s presidency - the fate of his legislative ambitions and the pressure of oversight investigations. It will also immediately set the stage for the 2028 presidential primaries, with both parties’ hopefuls reading the results for clues to the electorate’s mood. Here are four possible ways the midterms could broadly shake out. A blue wave In the House, Republicans hold the slimmest of majorities, with 218 seats (and one independent who caucuses with them) to the Democrats’ 214. The GOP is on defense in 16 seats rated toss-ups by the Cook Political Report, compared with six for Democrats. On Sept. 25, Cook shifted 15 races toward the Democrats and projected them to take over the House. Anticipating a favorable environment, Democrats went into the cycle planning to expand the House battlefield by recruiting competitive candidates to run in typically safe GOP districts held by incumbents unaccustomed to tough races or dragged down in scandals. On Friday, they continued widening their targets, adding eight districts that voted for Trump by double digits in 2024. They added six more races on Monday, including seats in Arkansas and Tennessee and a Nevada district that backed Trump by 14 points. The latest additions bring their total targets to 46. If Democrats win the popular vote by 10 points this year - their current average lead in polls - they would pick up a projected 33 seats, according to Mindset, a Washington advisory firm. That would place this year’s gains between the Democratic pickups in 2006 (31 seats) and 2018 (40 seats). “Democrats are on offense; Republicans are running scared - even in deep-red territory,” said Rep. Suzan DelBene (Washington), chair of the House Democrats’ campaign arm. “Voters are fed up with Republicans’ broken promises and ready for change in Congress.” In the Senate, Republicans hold a 53-47 majority and were favored to keep control earlier this year. Now, most polls put Democrats ahead in the most contested races: Alaska, Iowa, Maine, Michigan, New Hampshire, Ohio and Texas. They’re more strongly favored to win North Carolina, where former governor Roy Cooper (D) leads former Republican National Committee chairman Michael Whatley, and Georgia, where Rep. Mike Collins (R) hasn’t come close to catching Sen. Jon Ossoff (D). On Friday, the main Republican Senate super PAC canceled its remaining spending in North Carolina. Beyond the battlegrounds, Republicans have shown concern about incumbents in Kansas, which hasn’t elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1932, and Nebraska, which Trump won by 20 points in 2024. Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kansas), an obstetrician, is under fire for his history of suing patients to collect unpaid bills, leading to some arrests. He faces megachurch pastor Adam Hamilton (D). Nebraska independent Dan Osborn has been slamming Sen. Pete Ricketts (R) for pardoning a man convicted of sexual assault when he was governor. In the most extreme scenario, some political professionals imagine the wave wiping out Sen. Darline Graham (R-South Carolina) or Sen. Ashley Moody (R-Florida). A blue ripple The Senate does not as consistently turn against the president - Republicans added two seats in the upper chamber in 2018. This year’s map has more GOP-held seats in contention, but taking the majority would require the Democrats to hold Georgia and Michigan, pick up North Carolina and Maine, plus win two out of 12 seats in states that Trump won by at least 13 points. In the House, Democrats need a net gain of only three seats. But across decades, partisan gerrymandering has steadily shrunk the battlefield, so even an electoral swing of similar magnitude to past cycles might not flip as many seats. This cycle, Republicans tilted the field further in their direction by redrawing congressional maps ahead of the customary once-a-decade redistricting. Republicans hoped to move 16 districts to the right with new maps in Texas (five districts), Florida (four), Ohio (two), Alabama, Louisiana, Missouri, North Carolina and Tennessee (one each). Democrats responded with five districts in California, and courts overturned the Missouri map and added a Democratic-leaning seat in Utah, cutting the Republicans’ theoretical edge to nine. But many of those redrawn seats are shaping up to be less solid than Republicans had hoped. Democrats are still contesting four redrawn seats in Texas and another four in Florida. They hope to keep one or two affected districts in Ohio (held by Reps. Marcy Kaptur and Greg Landsman), plus the one in North Carolina (Rep. Don Davis). “People want to make predictions, but there’s a lot of toss-up races that are not decided yet,” Republican pollster John McLaughlin said. “The sides are forming where the Democratic/anti-Republican vote is coming together and Republicans are losing the ability to recover swing voters. That’s concerning.” A GOP upset In the previous midterms of 2022, the roles were reversed: Republicans were confident the unpopular sitting president would sweep their candidates into power despite their flaws, and were dismayed when that wave failed to materialize. Now, they are hoping for a similar dynamic, only the other way around. If Republicans pull an upset, they’ll be able to thank the Senate map that puts them mostly on their home turf and gerrymandering for padding their cushion in the House. The polls would have to be significantly off, which could be because Democrats were more eager to answer the phone, Republicans were less likely to participate, or pollsters misjudged who would turn out to vote. Trump political adviser Chris LaCivita summed up the Republicans’ path to victory as: “money, message, motivation and the president’s ability to defy conventional wisdom.” Republicans outspent Democrats in every Senate battleground in September and also led in future reservations though Election Day, according to media tracker AdImpact. Republicans are also hoping to benefit in races where further-left Democrats won their primaries. Those Democrats include Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan and House candidates William Lawrence in Michigan and Randy Villegas in California. The GOP’s midterms convention and Trump’s stump speeches have sought to portray the Democrats as extreme and tie the entire party to self-described socialists who won in some areas. And as much as Democrats want to make the race about Trump (and he does, too), at least some Republicans may be able to outperform his unpopularity. Candidates from Iowa to Florida have started removing references to Trump from their websites and breaking with the president on immigration and the Iran war. A constitutional crisis Elections are run at the local level, with no role for the federal government. The Trump administration has made multiple attempts to change voting procedures for the midterms, but those efforts were held up in court or died in Congress. “It has been a roller coaster,” Eric Fey, the Democratic elections director in St. Louis, said at a recent meeting of elections officials. Each election cycle features emergency litigation over mishaps at voting locations (often resulting in extended hours), recounts in close races and post-election audits. Administrators and law enforcement officials are also on the lookout for cyberattacks or disruptions such as bomb threats. They conduct drills and simulations to anticipate how things could go wrong and practice how to respond. “The threat landscape, as we view it this year, is cyber, physical, logistical, reputational and somewhat emergent legal,” said Michael Moore, the chief information security officer for the Arizona secretary of state’s office. “We design exercises to give election officials the most miserable Election Day we can possibly imagine. That way, when they actually have an election day, they’re prepared for everything.” This year, election administrators are especially concerned about interference from the federal government. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has said the administration has no plans to send immigration officers to polls, while FBI Director Kash Patel would not rule out sending his agents to voting sites. “While I anticipate that we likely will have monitors and there could be incidents at or around voting locations, we’re going to make sure that we have boots on the ground to make sure that voters are not disrupted in that process and that they can cast a ballot,” said Dean Logan, the registrar-recorder and county clerk for Los Angeles County, the country’s largest election jurisdiction. Monica Gordon, the clerk in Cook County, Illinois (home to Chicago), added: “We’re moving forward as usual, but we plan for anything. Our contingencies have contingencies.” Right-wing activists have called for Trump to take more severe steps, such as trying to claim emergency powers over elections. Trump has repeatedly challenged the legitimacy of elections he and his party lost. Congressional Democrats and allied lawyers have also prepared research and drills to be ready for any attempts to use federal power to interfere with the results, as Trump attempted after losing in 2020. “A lot of people would say that we need to just go rogue and declare this radical emergency,” Tina Peters, a former Colorado county clerk who was released on parole in June after serving some of her sentence for tampering with voting equipment, said Wednesday during a meeting of online activists. “There are already orders and laws in place that allow them to do what they need to do.” Related Content This article originally appeared on Washington Post at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/four-ways-midterm-elections-could-090000631.html

item.title: Pentagon officials' heated debates foreshadowed problems in Iran
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
As Houthi militants in Yemen attacked ships with missiles and drones in the Red Sea early last year, top U.S. officials gathered at the Pentagon to prepare military options for President Donald Trump. Their meetings repeatedly grew tense. On one side were Gen. Michael “Erik” Kurilla, then overseeing U.S. operations in the Middle East, and other hawks ready for action. The general was keen on military action not only against the Houthis but also against Iran, which had backed the Yemeni paramilitary group for years with weapons and training, according to people familiar with the matter. Like others, they spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss internal government deliberations. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. On the other side were officials hesitant to launch military strikes so early in the second Trump administration, including the Joint Chiefs chairman, Gen. Charles Q. Brown Jr., who suggested that new U.S. assessments of what military action might yield would be wise before presenting the president with military options. That triggered an abrupt response from Kurilla, people familiar with the matter said. “General,” Kurilla said, “the time for assessments is over.” The exchange, which has not previously been reported, surprised some in the room. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, then new to his role, agreed with Kurilla, people familiar with the matter said. The disagreement came as other Pentagon appointees, including then-senior adviser Dan Caldwell and policy official Alex Velez-Green, repeatedly raised questions in meetings about how an extended military campaign against the Houthis could deplete stocks of key U.S. munitions, the people familiar with the discussions said. That issue has since grown in prominence as the Trump administration burned through its arsenal of cruise missiles and interceptors in a war with Iran that is now seven months old. In recent weeks, the Iranian-backed Houthi militants have launched a new offensive in Yemen, seizing control of the strategically important Bab al-Mandab Strait, reigniting civil war and targeting critical energy infrastructure in Saudi Arabia. On Sunday, Yemen’s Saudi-backed government announced a military campaign to take back all land seized by the Houthis, who retaliated with a new wave of strikes against Saudi Arabia’s main oil company, Aramco. With Iran’s proxies weakened elsewhere, the group has emerged as the most powerful element of Tehran’s “Axis of Resistance” against the United States and Israel. In March 2025, weeks after the disagreement between the generals, Trump announced Operation Rough Rider, a 51-day bombing campaign against the Houthis that almost immediately was embroiled in scandal when then-White House national security adviser Mike Waltz accidentally invited a reporter into a group chat on Signal, the unclassified messaging application. More than 1,000 targets were hit over the course of Rough Rider, including key Houthi commanders and weapons stocks. But the aerial bombing also resulted in significant civilian casualties, human rights groups said. Trump and Hegseth touted the campaign as a resounding success, but other senior Pentagon officials, including Caldwell and Joe Kasper, Hegseth’s first chief of staff, questioned whether the campaign had clear and obtainable objectives, the people familiar with deliberations said. The U.S. went on to strike Iran’s nuclear facilities in Operation Midnight Hammer in June 2025 and, along with Israel, launched a sprawling war against Iran this February. A spokesperson for Hegseth, Kingsley Wilson, said in a statement that Rough Rider “achieved decisive success against Houthi forces,” with U.S. forces launching strikes that “severely degraded radar networks, air-defense systems, ballistic-missile and drone launch sites, weapons depots, and production facilities while removing multiple mid- and senior-level commanders from the battlefield.” The military action, Wilson added, “substantially reduced immediate threats to vital international shipping lanes, compelled a clear tactical shift by the adversary, and helped create conditions for a ceasefire that strengthened freedom of navigation in the region.” She declined to comment on the possibility of any future action in Yemen, but she said the Pentagon’s role is to “develop and present military options to the President, and he makes the final choice.” The White House and the Pentagon both released statements defending the management of weapons stockpiles after The Washington Post shared its reporting that some administration officials had concerns about it before Rough Rider began. U.S. officials have said that while the U.S. military has a deep arsenal of weapons, it is increasingly running low on specific munitions, such as ship-launched Tomahawk cruise missiles and Patriot air-defense interceptors. “The United States Military has enough munitions and ammo to serve all of the Commander-in-Chief’s strategic goals and beyond,” White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly wrote in a statement. Kasper and Caldwell declined to comment, while Velez-Green could not be reached for comment. Kurilla, who retired in August 2025, did not respond to requests for comment about the exchange with Brown or the objectives of Rough Rider. Brown declined to comment through a spokesperson, but a person familiar with his thinking said he did not dispute the account of the testy Pentagon deliberations. It’s common, that person said, for a top commander to push for quick military action while the Joint Chiefs chairman considers a wider range of issues, including making sure all necessary plans and requirements are in place and that the president’s options are preserved. Brown was fired and forced into retirement just before Rough Rider, as Hegseth pushed to remove top Biden-era generals. An official with Hegseth’s office declined to say whether Brown’s caution about the Houthis played a role, saying that “out of respect for our senior military leaders,” they do not discuss “the nature of their retirements.” An abrupt ceasefire The military campaign in Yemen abruptly ended in May 2025 with a ceasefire brokered by Oman. Trump claimed victory and said that the Houthis “don’t want to fight anymore.” “They gave us their word that they wouldn’t be shooting at ships anymore, and we honor that,” Trump said. The end of combat operations, officials and analysts said, came after the Houthis showed remarkable resiliency in the face of American airpower. No U.S. troops were killed during the operation, but the militants shot down at least seven MQ-9 Reaper drones, and U.S. forces lost two F/A-18 fighter jets in mishaps at sea. The operation, people familiar with the effort said, was followed by the administration’s near-total abandonment of Yemen. “It was like … a cord being pulled out of a socket,” said a former U.S. official who worked on Yemen issues at the time. Trump “wanted to scratch Yemen off the list and move on.” When the mission was declared over, the former official said, some in U.S. Central Command, which Kurilla then oversaw, were “apoplectic,” believing that they had been making progress. A U.S. special envoy position for Yemen issues was never filled by the Trump administration, and Washington’s assistance to the impoverished country was slashed. At the time, the former official said, they warned colleagues: “You ignore Yemen at your own peril.” ‘Folkloric status’ The disagreements at the Pentagon about how to proceed on Yemen underscore the competing views in the U.S. government about how to handle the persistent threat the Houthis have posed since they seized power in northern Yemen in 2014. The Shiite militia, which formed in the 1990s, aims to control Yemen, a country of 35 million at the southwest tip of the Arabian Peninsula. From 2015 to 2022, the Houthis, with support from Iran, fought a bloody civil war against Yemen’s internationally recognized government, which is backed by Saudi Arabia. That war ended with a fragile truce that left the Houthis holding large swaths of the country’s north and the government coalition in control of the south. But the group has much larger ambitions, including ousting the U.S. from the Middle East and destroying the state of Israel. April Longley Alley, a senior fellow at the Washington Institute, said that Houthis “see themselves as the tip of the spear in the Arab world.” Dan Shapiro, who served as U.S. ambassador to Israel during the Obama administration, described the Houthis as “an enduring problem” for decades to come. “We’re kind of stuck with this bad actor on this maritime choke point, able to activate and try to use their position or leverage at the moment of their choosing,” said Shapiro, who later became a Pentagon official during the Biden administration. After the Hamas attacks on Oct. 7, 2023, the Houthis started firing missiles at Israel in retaliation for the resulting military campaign in Gaza. That is when the Houthis took on an almost “folkloric status,” said Tim Lenderking, the U.S. envoy to Yemen during the Biden administration. “It really bolstered their standing and their brand in the Arab world,” he added. But the Houthis took it too far, he said, firing on U.S. and Israeli ships, killing international mariners and disrupting the flow of commercial traffic in the Red Sea. The Biden administration launched military strikes against the Houthis beginning in January 2024. The Houthis appeared undeterred. Trump launched Rough Rider on March 15, 2025. A few days later, he declared that “tremendous damage” had been inflicted on the “Houthi barbarians” and would get worse. “It’s not even a fair fight, and never will be,” Trump wrote in a social media post. “They will be completely annihilated!” Unclear objectives, mounting costs The costs and questions quickly mounted. Over the course of the operation, estimated at more than $1 billion, the Houthis continued to target U.S. warships in the Red Sea and surrounding waterways. U.S. forces struck a migrant detention center in Yemen in April 2025, reportedly killing more than 68 civilians and injuring dozens more, according to Human Rights Watch. The operation also was dogged by the “Signalgate” scandal, in which senior Trump administration officials, including Hegseth and Vice President JD Vance, communicated about Rough Rider in a group chat that accidentally included Atlantic journalist Jeffrey Goldberg. The revelation was especially damaging for Hegseth, who had shared specific, advance details about how the bombing would begin through the unclassified Signal app. A review by the Pentagon inspector general released in December found that Hegseth’s actions “created a risk to operational security,” though the secretary of defense and his team claimed “total exoneration.” The Trump administration began looking for an exit from Rough Rider just a couple of weeks into the bombing campaign, said Alley of the Washington Institute. There had been an assumption going into the campaign that “you could go in and coerce the Houthis with overwhelming power to change [their] behavior.” But Trump lacked a clear exit strategy, Alley said, so when Oman - long a mediator in the region - approached the administration saying that the Houthis wanted a truce, Trump took it. One of the people familiar with internal deliberations at the Pentagon said that the abrupt end to Rough Rider bolstered the belief among internal critics that the offensive’s objectives were never clear in the first place. “It almost seemed,” this person said, “that Trump had buyer’s remorse.” The deal, Trump said at the time, was simple: The Houthis would stop firing at U.S. ships if the U.S. stopped firing at the Houthis. “We hit them very hard and they had a great ability to withstand punishment,” Trump said in announcing the ceasefire. “You could say there was a lot of bravery there.” ‘They rebuilt it all’ Yemen’s Saudi-backed coalition government was supportive of Rough Rider and caught off guard when it ended, according to a Yemeni official, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity of the situation. “The Trump administration did not read the situation strategically,” said the official. “They just wanted a quick win.” It was not long, the person said, before the Houthis “rebuilt everything.” In recent weeks, the Houthis have repeatedly attacked oil infrastructure and military bases in Saudi Arabia, which also saw its key East-West oil pipeline attacked by Iraqi militias. As Saudi Arabia - long a key U.S. ally - faces its biggest threats in years, it has confronted Trump’s unwillingness to get more involved and looked to new partners for help in confronting the Houthis. Saudi Arabia and its allies in Yemen’s government fought on Monday to take back land along Yemen’s western coast to regain control of Bab al-Mandab, in a counteroffensive that analysts said could substantially deepen the conflict. Nadwa Al-Dawsari, a Yemeni researcher and conflict analyst, said the Trump administration never should have seen the truce as a win. “The Houthis have learned how to use negotiations, ceasefires and truces as a tactic to preserve their power, rebuild their capabilities and prepare for the next round of conflict,” she said. Houthi spokesperson Mohammed Abdulsalam said that Rough Rider “sparked widespread resentment regarding the U.S.” and led to an influx of volunteers. Yemen, he said in a written statement to The Post, is known as the “graveyard of invaders.” “Anyone who has attempted to colonize or occupy the country,” he said, “has left burdened by woes, sorrow, failure, and defeat.” Trump struck a conciliatory tone in recent weeks when talking about the Houthis, saying last month in Ireland that the Houthis “called us, and they don’t want to fight us.” “Everything will work out very well,” he said. The Yemeni official said that they fear the Trump administration still does not understand the threat that the Houthis pose, noting that the group is already working extensively with al-Shabab in Somalia and has clearly stated intentions to push the U.S. out of the region and destroy the state of Israel. “The lesson I learned over the past 10 years is to take the Houthis seriously,” the official added. “I am not sure if the United States learned the same lesson.” Alley said that Trump’s decision last year to forge a truce with the Houthis had the unintended consequence of showing the militant group the limits of Trump’s willingness to escalate - giving them additional room to maneuver. “Trump may be done with the Houthis,” she said, “but the Houthis are not done with Trump.” Susannah George contributed to this report. Related Content This article originally appeared on Washington Post at https://washingtonpost.com/world/2026/10/05/pentagon-dispute-trumps-first-war-foreshadowed-iran-challenges/

item.title: Guns, voting, immigration and more: The biggest cases the Supreme Court will take up in its new term
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The Supreme Court began its latest term on Monday with a docket full of high-stakes cases that touch on some of the most contentious issues in American politics, including guns, voting and transgender rights. This will be the second full term for the nation's highest court since President Trump returned to the White House. The previous term, which wrapped up in June, was packed with landmark rulings in a long list of major cases , including Trump's tariffs, birthright citizenship and a slate of key immigration decisions. The justices will likely take on additional cases over the course of the term, but there are already plenty of pivotal cases for the court to consider in the coming months. Here's a rundown of the big cases headed to the Supreme Court this term and what their eventual rulings might mean for the country. Guns Over the past two decades, the Supreme Court has issued a series of decisions that have significantly expanded gun rights. It could go even further next term when it considers whether laws banning certain semiautomatic rifles , like the AR-15, violate the Second Amendment. This category of guns was banned nationwide for a decade until Congress allowed the law to expire in 2004. Similar bans are currently in place in about a dozen states. Gun rights groups have challenged those laws , arguing that it's unconstitutional for these specific types of firearms to be singled out for bans that don't apply to other guns under the Second Amendment. Citizen voting A dozen states currently require voters to show proof of citizenship — like a birth certificate or passport — when they register to vote. The Supreme Court will consider the legality of these requirements again, this time in a challenge to Arizona's latest proof-of-citizenship law in the case Republican National Committee v. Mi Familia Vota . The law is currently blocked by a federal circuit court ruling that called some of its provisions "unlawful measures of voter suppression." Republicans have asked the court to overturn that decision and allow the requirements in Arizona and elsewhere to remain in place. The court's final ruling could have massive implications for voting across the United States. Non-citizen voting is extraordinarily rare and there are already legal measures in place in every state to ensure that only ballots from citizens are counted. That hasn't stopped Republicans from pushing for new laws requiring voters to prove their citizenship. Ballot measures aimed at curbing noncitizen voting will be considered by voters in six states in November. Trump's signature elections bill, the SAVE America Act, would apply the requirements nationwide. Some researchers argue that, rather than preventing fraud, these laws create hurdles that prevent eligible voters from casting their ballots. According to one estimate, as many as 21 million people across the United States lack the documents they would need to be able to vote under proof-of-citizenship requirements. Transgender rights One of the many points of debate around transgender rights in recent years has been the extent of parents' authority over decisions involving their trans-identifying children. The court will weigh in on this issue once again this term when it hears a case challenging a Washington law that gives the operators of emergency shelters the option not to contact parents of runaway transgender youth who are seeking gender-affirming care. A group of parents has sued, arguing that the law violates their parental rights "to raise their child in accordance with the child's biological sex." The pending case runs along similar lines to one decided earlier this year, in which the justices ruled in favor of parents seeking to block a California law that limited when schools can "out" transgender students to their families. Schools In 2020, Colorado voters approved a ballot measure to establish universal preschool throughout the state. As part of the program, state funding is only available to private preschools that meet certain "equal opportunity" standards — including a willingness to enroll LGBTQ students. Two Catholic preschools sued the state , arguing that they were being discriminated against on the basis of their religion by being denied state funding for standing by their beliefs. The state contends that there is no discrimination present because its rules apply to all schools, whether they're religiously affiliated or not. In two similar cases over the past decade, the court has come down on the side of the schools, ruling that states generally can't exclude religious schools from public programs simply because they are religious. Immigration After siding with Trump in a series of immigration-related rulings during its most recent term, the court has agreed to take on three more cases that touch on the heart of the president's immigration agenda. The headline case, which the court agreed to hear just a few days before the start of the term, centers around the Trump administration's mandatory detention policy for undocumented immigrants. Historically, migrants who are being considered for removal have had the opportunity to apply for release from detention while they wait for their case to be decided by the courts. Trump changed that policy, causing tens of thousands of immigrants to remain in detention while they await potential deportation. Lower courts have split on the question of whether it's legal for the administration to uniformly deny detained migrants the right to a bond hearing. Now, the Supreme Court will have the final say. A second case centers around Trump's migrant detention policies for a different group of immigrants. The central question is whether migrants with a criminal history, including those who were in the country legally, can be held in detention centers indefinitely, or if they have the right to challenge their detention in court. The case involves two lawful permanent residents who were detained for what they argue was an "unreasonably prolonged" period without a bond hearing. Immigration detention has become a major source of debate during Trump's second term, amid reports of unsafe conditions at detention centers and a striking increase in the number of deaths among detainees. The third immigration case involves immigrants who had once been granted asylum in the United States, had that status revoked and now argue that they should be eligible to become lawful permanent residents. The government argues, and lower courts have agreed so far, that only immigrants with active asylum protection can apply for a green card. Climate change Over the past few years, the Supreme Court has significantly narrowed the government's power to regulate greenhouse emissions in a series of landmark rulings. Next term, it will take up another case that could close off yet another pathway that municipalities have used to try to fight climate change. Lawmakers in Boulder, Colo., have sued oil and gas companies for their role in perpetuating climate change. Those companies have asked the Supreme Court to block the lawsuit. They contend, and the Trump administration agrees , that only the federal government has the power to seek these types of damages because the impacts of climate change go far beyond Boulder's jurisdiction. Several other cities and some states have filed similar suits against the fossil fuel industry. The court could invalidate all of them if it rules in the companies' favor. Jury trials The court will decide whether juries in criminal trials must have 12 jurors . That's already the law in most of the country, but a half-dozen states allow for as few as six jurors in certain cases. The case centers around Hamed Kian, a Florida chiropractor who was convicted of practicing after his license had been suspended following allegations of inappropriate contact with patients. Kian's attorneys argue that the small jury violated his constitutional right to a fair and speedy trial. item.title: Sam Altman: ‘The world should accept some bad things happening’ for benefits of AI
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman admits “something’s clearly not working” with the artificial intelligence money that has flooded the midterm elections — and he doesn’t expect President Donald Trump’s rebrand of the technology to improve his industry’s image with the American public, either. “I get why AI has a really negative perception right now,” Altman told Brendan Bordelon in an exclusive interview marking the launch of Decoded by POLITICO . “I don’t think spending money on politics is what’s going to make people feel better about it. The industry needs to figure out a way to address what the actual concerns are, and right now, a lot of people in the industry are being quite tone deaf.” In the wide-ranging conversation, Altman offered a window into how OpenAI is confronting new political pressures and intensified competition with Anthropic, its corporate archrival run by former employee Dario Amodei. Altman says OpenAI is more tolerant than Anthropic of less-than-catastrophic harms from AI, drawing out what he sees as a fundamental split in worldview between the two leading labs even as they converge on tougher rules in the wake of high-profile autonomous hacking incidents. “We believe that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology and people having the agency,” said Altman, who characterized those harms as linked to “the lighter touch regulatory stance that we advocate for.” “I wouldn't take a trade of saying like, ‘We'll make sure there's no major hacks, there's no kind of like misuse of this technology, there's zero scams, there's zero all the other bad things that will happen,’” said Altman. “Because I think people will do tremendously orders of magnitude more good stuff.” The OpenAI head also suggested there needs to be a new “liability framework” for companies whose models are capable of autonomous cyberattacks, like the Hugging Face hack over the summer and incidents involving government websites. Altman called that behavior “clearly unacceptable,” and said that “if something goes wrong with our models during training, there's going to be some version of that we need to be responsible for.” “This is the kind of thing that we are hoping our policymakers will all debate,” he added, as Congress remains deadlocked. And while Altman defended a “morally binding” AI safety accord that Trump signed with tech CEOs last week as a great start for the industry, he predicted calls for guardrails will continue and said he would “welcome something more.” He also said he shares the concerns of those who worry AI rules are being crafted by the White House and tech executives without input from Congress or the public. “If we do too much to restrict this technology in the name of safety, and we end up with a small number of companies or people — or perhaps one country — that have too much power over this, that also is a way that this can go horribly wrong,” Altman said. Trump paired last week’s AI agreement with an executive order renaming artificial intelligence to “super intelligence.” It’s a term Altman considers more accurate, though he doubts the public will find it “less scary.” He expects people to keep using “AI” — and unlike Elon Musk , he won’t be renaming OpenAI to OpenSI. “Brands are sticky,” Altman said. Throughout the interview, Altman sought to explain his company’s new policy posture. He recently agreed with Amodei on the need to slow down AI’s development, and his lobbyists have increasingly followed Anthropic in backing new safety requirements at all levels of government. But despite emphasizing “a lot of daylight” between OpenAI and Anthropic, Altman also tried to distance himself — on both policy and politics — from the Silicon Valley investors who are spending heavily to block strict regulations, including through the pro-AI super PAC network Leading the Future . “When it comes to the potential of a serious loss of control to AI … this is where I would say to the accelerationists, let’s be a little thoughtful about lurching into this future,” he said, using a descriptor often applied to the tech leaders and advisers who have Trump’s ear on AI. item.title: Saudi-led coalition says its jets are bombing Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
ADEN, Yemen (AP) — Forces of Yemen's internationally recognized government began a major offensive Monday against the Iranian-backed Houthi rebels on the country's Red Sea coast, under an intensified air campaign by the Saudi-led coalition. The offensive came just after the rebels said they had captured more territory in the southwestern part of Yemen, taking a key town in a blow to the Saudi-backed forces as they advanced toward a strategic provincial capital in the region. The Saudi-led coalition spokesman, Maj. Gen. Turki al-Malki, said 100 fighter jets were providing support to the forces of Yemen's internationally recognized government fighting against the Houthis. He said the coalition has secured "air protection" of the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait and destroyed hundreds of Houthi targets as part of the ongoing campaign. The campaign and its details could not be immediately independently verified. Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters that it was expected that the Saudi-backed government in Yemen would hit back at the rebels to reclaim territory. Asked if the Saudi-led coalition coordinated the action with the United States, Rubio said that Saudi Arabia and the U.S. have a defense agreement but wouldn't offer more details. He said the Yemeni government was ousted from some of its territory by a Houthi campaign and the Saudis have come under attack, and "they have a right to defend themselves." The U.S. has provided support to Saudi Arabia in its ongoing campaign against the Houthis, according to a regional official and a U.S. official. This U.S. support included intelligence sharing, target identification and planning for the offensive, said the officials who spoke on condition of anonymity because they weren't authorized to speak to reporters. The U.S. had supported the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis early in the Yemen war, before quitting the coalition in recent years. The air campaign follows the fall of a key town in Yemen The Houthi rebels seized the town of Turbah on Sunday, shortly before the internationally recognized government announced a major military operation against them. The escalation between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis has revived Yemen's civil war after a four-year ceasefire. Turbah sits on a main road linking the provincial capital of Taiz with the port city of Aden, which serves as an interim seat of Yemen's government. Over the years, the town was a major post for the government forces defending Taiz against the Houthis. Earlier, the Houthis seized several villages and areas on Taiz's outskirts in a series of advances, paving the way for the rebels to encircle Taiz, Yemen's third-largest city. Yemen's flare-up shows the capabilities of the Iran-backed rebels The Houthis made a swift push on the country's western coast on the Red Sea in early September. They captured the strategic city of Mokha and several Red Sea islands, gains that enabled them to control the Yemeni side of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a crucial chokepoint through which 12% of global trade transits. In its announcement Sunday, the Saudi-backed government said it was mobilizing troops across government-held areas. Rashad al-Alimi, head of the ruling Presidential Leadership Council, said in a televised speech that the operations were aiming at "recovering the remaining territories" controlled by the Houthis. He called on the international community to provide support to his government. Hours after al-Alimi's declaration, a Saudi military spokesperson, Maj. Gen. Turki al-Malki, vowed "full operational support" to the Yemeni government forces, until the Houthis are "eliminated." Al-Malki also stressed Saudi Arabia's right to take all necessary measures to deter the rebels who continued to fire missiles and drones at the kingdom as part of the nearly three-month escalation that revived Yemen's civil war. Saudi-backed government forces are trying to fight back On Monday, factions allied with the Saudi-backed coalition fighting the Houthis said they launched offensives against the rebels on the eastern flank of the coastal areas that the Houthis had seized in their latest advances. They attacked Houthi positions in the town of Dhubab, on the coast of the Bab el-Mandeb strait, said Col. Majed al-Nazili, spokesman for the Saudi-backed forces. The Giants Brigades, a government-allied group, said it began a "decisive military operation against the Houthi militias," also in the Bab el-Mandeb area. Al-Alimi said in a post on X on Monday that the operation — dubbed "Yemen Dawn" — has started with the aim of "restoring state institutions, liberating" Sanaa, Yemen's rebel-controlled capital, and ending "the Houthi terrorist militia coup." Al-Nazili said government forces were carrying out a "strategic offensive" on Sanaa. The Houthi media office reported multiple airstrikes by the Saudi coalition on their territories, including Sanaa. The latest flare-up began in mid-July, when the Houthis accused Saudi Arabia of bombing the airport in Sanaa to prevent the landing of an unauthorized Iranian flight. The rebels responded with missile and drone attacks against Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government forces in the country. They also announced a blockade on Saudi shipping in the Red Sea and attacked several Saudi-linked vessels. Then in September, they intensified their campaign, storming down the Red Sea coast in their biggest land grab in years. The rebels' taking of Turbah "will likely severely constrain Yemeni government-aligned forces' ability to reinforce and resupply front-line positions" across Taiz province and the provincial capital of Taiz, according to the Institute for the Study of War, a Washington-based think tank. "Disrupting resupply has military value, of course, but controlling all the roads in and out of areas to the north of Turbah also prevents government forces from retreating out of the city," the think tank wrote in a Sunday analysis. The escalation has revamped Yemen's 12-year civil war Yemen's civil war began in 2014 when the Houthis descended from their northern stronghold, capturing Sanaa and forcing the government to flee into exile in Saudi Arabia. The war created one of the world's worst humanitarian disasters and killed more than 150,000 people. The latest bout of violence has killed at least 959 people and wounded over 4,200 others, according to the World Health Organization. The flare-up forced about 174,097 people to flee their homes inside Yemen, according to the U.N. migration agency. More than 3,000 others fled across the waters into Djibouti, the agency reported. Last week, Yemen's health ministry — part of the internationally recognized government — warned about the conflict's impact on health facilities and medical staff across Taiz province. The ministry said in a statement on Friday that health facilities in coastal, western and southern areas of the province have closed or are barely partially functioning. ___ Magdy reported from Cairo. Associated Press writer Matthew Lee contributed to this report. item.title: FBI arrests suspected Chinese agent accused of surveilling Taiwan president's son
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The FBI arrested a suspected Chinese agent at Los Angeles International Airport after she allegedly surveilled the Taiwanese president's U.S.-based son, law enforcement sources told CBS News. Wanying "Heather" Zhang, an Irvine, California, realtor, was cuffed by federal law enforcement on Sunday before she boarded a flight to Shanghai, China, from LAX, on a charge of acting as an unregistered agent of a foreign government. Zhang's husband Edric Ding, a realtor at the same firm, told CBS News when reached by phone Sunday: "I don't know anything yet," and declined to comment further. It was not immediately clear if Zhang has an attorney. A criminal complaint, filed in federal court by a member of the FBI's counterintelligence squad in L.A., accused Zhang and an accomplice of traveling to Seattle, Washington, in September 2025 and taking pictures at the suburban home of a top Taiwanese official's family. Law enforcement sources told CBS News that the target was Ting-Yu Lai, the son of Taiwanese President Ching-Te Lai. Ting-Yu, an engineer in his 30s, attended college in America and has a young U.S.-born son with his wife, Hsiao Chen, according to Taiwanese media reports. He now works for the Dutch multinational electronics firm Philips. "If the PRC [People's Republic of China] wish to obtain leverage over the President of Taiwan during any potential conflict, the location and pictures of the close relatives of a high-ranking Taiwanese government official, including pictures of their homes and cars, could be useful to the PRC," wrote FBI Special Agent Kevin Holt in the Oct. 3, 2026, criminal complaint. Taiwan has been the focus of high geopolitical tensions for decades . It asserts its independence, while the Chinese government claims it is part of China. The island is in a key position astride major shipping lanes, and is where many of the world's most advanced semiconductor chips are manufactured. CBS News reached out to the Taiwanese consulate for comment. The complaint said Zhang, 34, and a man named only as "Individual 1" flew from Las Vegas to Seattle on Sept. 1, 2025, rented a black Nissan Rogue and drove to their target's home. Images from a neighbor's security camera included in the complaint allegedly show the two "appearing to film" Ting-Yu, his wife and their child as they arrived home that evening. CBS News matched the images to an address near Seattle owned by Ting-Yu. Zhang allegedly texted her Chinese government handler: "Saw him. Young male. It's that young one," and "I am videorecording," followed by two license plate numbers, according to the complaint. The FBI agent wrote that the texts from the Chinese messaging app WeChat were obtained from a search warrant on Zhang's iCloud account. "Zhang was in contact with at least two people whom she appeared to acknowledge worked for the PRC government," the agent wrote. The complaint claims Zhang was introduced in June 2025 to one of the Chinese government officials by a classmate from her alma mater, Beijing's University of International Relations, which Holt said has close ties to the Ministry of State Security. Holt's affidavit claims Zhang booked a private room in Changsha, China, during a June 2025 trip, where she allegedly met the government official and received her surveillance mission. She later texted the official, "I can take care of this thing," according to the complaint. On Aug. 26, 2025, Zhang wrote: "I will be busy with work in L.A. this week. I will probably go to Seattle next week," and the official replied: "Ok. Thank you for your hard work," the complaint said. Zhang is a licensed California realtor with JC Pacific Capital Inc. Her Zillow profile says she has 130 sales and listings around Los Angeles and neighboring counties. Ting-Yu received his bachelor's in electrical engineering from Case Western Reserve University in Cleveland, Ohio, in 2012; a master's in Bioengineering Innovation and Design from Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore, the following year; then a PhD from the Department of Bioengineering at the University of Washington, according to a profile from one of his academic publications. Taiwan TV news station SETN reported that he met his Taiwanese wife while studying for his doctorate. They married in 2018 and had a child in the U.S. in 2020, according to CNA , Taiwan's national news agency. Chinese government agents have previously been caught spying on and harassing Chinese dissidents and pro-democracy activists in the U.S. Federal prosecutors said Shujun Wang , 75, infiltrated and informed on a Chinese pro-democracy group in Queens, New York, for the Chinese Ministry of State Security for 17 years. He was convicted in 2024 of acting as a foreign agent. Two people were arrested in April 2023 for their involvement in an unofficial Chinese police station in Manhattan set up to monitor Chinese dissidents. The Justice Department has warned of a plan by the Chinese security services called Operation Fox Hunt aimed at repatriating wanted Chinese nationals around the world, which targets enemies of the regime. New York-based Quanzhong An, who prosecutors say is a leader of the U.S. wing of Operation Fox Hunt, was sentenced in March 2025 after harassing a Chinese dissident in an attempt to bring them back to China. In California, former Arcadia Mayor Eileen Wang was charged with acting as a Chinese agent in May. She admitted to being paid to spread pro-Chinese government propaganda in the U.S., including an essay on her blog denying "forced labor" in China. item.title: U.S. removes B-1 bombers from U.K. air base after new security threat
item.description:

A Rockwell B1 Lancer heavy bomber takes off from RAF Fairford in Fairford, United Kingdom, on October 04. - David Bown/Getty Images The United States moved all of its long-range bombers stationed in the United Kingdom back to their American home bases on Sunday after an unspecified new threat, according to a US official. It comes days after the British government arrested a number of individuals in connection with an alleged Iranian plot to target the UK airbase where the planes had been stationed. “We can acknowledge now that all US bombers that were deployed to RAF Fairford have re-deployed to their home stations in the United States,” the official told CNN. The statement did not include details on why the planes were moved. The source familiar called the latest threat a “real world incident.” It is unusual that the US military would move the bombers back to their home stations instead of deploying them to another base in the region, the official said. Vice President JD Vance said Monday that the move was made “out of an abundance of caution,” suggesting it was a response to a potential threat from Iran even as he declined to detail the specific concerns. “I think that we’re going to be as careful as we possibly can be,” Vance told reporters. “We do feel with some confidence that the Iranians are, you know, they’re trying to do what the Iranian state has done for 49 years, which is engage in acts of terrorism against the United States and against a lot of other people as well.” US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, meanwhile, downplayed the removal of the US bombers, saying he would not “directly tie” the planes’ redeployment to the alleged Iranian plot. “The only reason why you guys are focused on how many planes are at Fairford is because of the threat that happened last week. But it’s not unusual to see rotations happen and movement of assets to different parts of the world based on exercises, redeployments, people changing out and new people coming in, new planes coming in, old planes going out,” Rubio told reporters at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland on Monday. Rubio added that the United States had worked closely on security with the UK for a long time, including on the Fairford investigation. A Downing Street spokesperson said that the UK government would not comment on foreign nations’ military operations. Asked about safety concerns by residents living near the base, the spokesperson told reporters that the UK has “the tried and tested approaches to defend our bases around the country, but not just that, throughout the world.” The UK Ministry of Defense also declined to comment on the operations or capabilities of other nations. The Royal Air Force base at Fairford has been used to deploy US B-1 bombers involved in the war against Iran and is an operating location for US Global Strike Command, which is tasked with managing long-distance strikes. CNN national security analyst Alex Plitsas said it was likely several dozen bombers were stationed at Fairford, adding that it was unusual to move all the aircraft. “It speaks to the credibility and the seriousness of the threat overall to the base that we’re talking about,” he told Ben Hunte on CNN Newsroom. The relocation of the bombers comes amid the investigation into the alleged plot. British police on September 27 arrested five men on suspicion of terror and explosives offenses close to the airbase. The men – identified only as British nationals between the ages of 23 and 25 and from the London area – were quickly released on bail, with police confirming no explosives were found in three vans at the scene. Their release sparked criticism from President Donald Trump, who said “I wouldn’t have done that.” A 25-year-old British-Iranian dual national was also arrested on Thursday in connection with the alleged plot. British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said last week there are “strong indications” Iran was involved in the incident. “We will say more in due course, but we can confirm our belief that we believe Iran to have played a part,” he told the BBC on Sept 30. Burnham’s remarks appeared to support the US’ assessment that the incident involved a foreign actor. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said “the hands of a foreign actor” were involved in the alleged plot but declined to provide details in an interview with Fox News last week. “I think it ties us to the reality here. We are dealing with elements in the world, and in the case of Iran for example, who have openly threatened to attack American interests globally,” he said. Meanwhile, Iran has denied any involvement in the incident, described the accusations as baseless and summoned the British ambassador in Tehran, Iranian state media reported Thursday. During the meeting, Iran’s Deputy Foreign Minister Majid Takht-Ravanchi reportedly urged London to revise what he called its “inappropriate approach” toward Tehran. This has been updated with additional details. CNN’s Nic Robertson, Max Saltman, Chandler Thornton Tim Lister and James Frater contributed to this report. TOKYO (AP) — The arrest of a U.S. Marine on suspicion of robbing and killing a local woman on Okinawa has drawn condemnation from Japan's leaders and renewed protests against the heavy American military presence on the southern island. He has denied the allegations, according to Japanese media. Ballard was arrested when a patrolling officer saw him walking later Saturday in an entertainment district in Okinawa City, about 25 kilometers (15 miles) northeast of Naha. His shaved head and the tattoos on his arms matched those of the man in security footage, Kyodo news agency reported. “I’m outraged and flabbergasted to hear that a suspect came to the (entertainment area) after committing a murder,” Kenji Higa, who lives in Okinawa City, told the Okinawa Times. There is longstanding anger over the behavior of some Americans People in Okinawa have long been wary of the U.S. presence on the island but many have come to see its strategic value due to what is widely viewed as a growing threat from China. Okinawa was under U.S. occupation from World War II until 1972. Today it hosts 70% of America’s military facilities and most of the 50,000 U.S. troops based in Japan today. There has been anger over increasing crime linked to the U.S. military on the island. The number of U.S. military-related criminal cases rose to 101 last year from about 40 in 2020, according to prefectural police. After the 1995 rape of a 12-year-old girl by three U.S. service members, huge crowds protested the heavy U.S. troop presence on Okinawa. There was also anger over the rape of a teenage girl by a U.S. service member in 2024 and the delayed disclosure of the crime. About 160 people gathered at a protest Sunday in Naha, condemning the crime and renewing demands that U.S. military bases be removed from the island. One sign read: “We’ve had enough of this!” Japanese officials condemn the crime “The case deals a major shock and adds fear to the Okinawans who have already been forced to live next to U.S. bases,” newly elected Okinawa Gov. Genta Koja told reporters Sunday night in Naha. “It is absolutely unforgivable and we are outraged.” Koja said the case underscored the ineffectiveness of past disciplinary measures taken by the U.S. military following similar crimes. “I’m enraged by the loss of a precious life of an Okinawan resident,” Koja told Lt. Gen. Benjamin Watson, commander of III Marine Expeditionary Force, and U.S. Consul General in Naha, Andrew Ou on Monday when he summoned them to the prefectural government. He demanded that U.S. officials take effective preventive measures. Watson replied: “I recognize the serious incident caused significant concern and anxiety among the residents of Okinawa, our neighbors” and that “we are committed to being good neighbors … and earning the trust of the Okinawan people.” In Tokyo, Takaichi condemned the crime and demanded full cooperation and tougher disciplinary and preventive measures by the United States. Japanese prosecutors started examining the suspect's case on Monday to determine whether to press formal charges in coming weeks. If convicted, he could face life in prison or the death penalty. Vamos said such disputes over warrants were not uncommon - but if the police lost on a technical error, they could still sometimes keep what they had obtained in a search. After Mountbatten-Windsor's arrest in February he was taken to Aylsham police station. item.title: Former Republican House speaker Dennis Hastert dead at 84
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Washington — Former Speaker of the House Dennis Hastert, who represented Illinois for two decades in Congress and was jailed for violating banking laws, has died, a coroner in Illinois said. He was 84. Both the longest-serving Republican House speaker and the highest-ranking elected U.S. official to serve a prison sentence, Hastert's stunning fall from grace came in 2016, when he was sentenced to 15 months in prison on charges related to his concealment of hush money payments made to cover up his sexual abuse of teenage boys during his time as a high school wrestling coach. Kendall County Coroner Jacquie Purcell confirmed Monday that Hastert died at his home over the weekend due to natural causes. No further details were given. Born in 1942 in Aurora, Illinois, Hastert grew up in a farming community. He went on to graduate from Wheaton College, where he received a degree in economics, before earning a teaching degree from Northern Illinois University. Hastert married Jean Kahl in 1973. The couple had two sons. Hastert worked as a teacher in Illinois for 16 years while coaching wrestling. In 1976, he was named Illinois Coach of the Year. Four decades later, he would admit to sexually abusing boys during his time as a coach. Hastert then served in the Illinois legislature, before going on to be elected to represent Illinois' 14th district in the U.S. House in 1986. Hastert served in Congress from 1987 to 2007. With the mentorship of House Minority Leader Robert. H Michel, Hastert's profile grew among the GOP ranks, and in 1995, he became chief deputy whip. When former House Speaker Newt Gingrich stepped down in 1998, Hastert became the conference's second choice for his successor, following Rep. Bob Livingston's decision to step aside amid a scandal over extra-marital affairs. Known as the "accidental speaker," Hastert would go on to become the longest-serving Republican speaker in history. During his tenure, Hastert, who had been a vocal critic of the Clinton administration, worked closely with former President George W. Bush on his policy agenda. Among Hastert's most enduring imprints on the chamber is the rule that bears his name, which informally requires that the House vote only on measures that have a majority of support from the majority party in the chamber. The rule, which has faced criticism for making Congress more partisan, has posed hurdles for Republican House leadership in recent years. After House Republicans lost the majority in the 2006 midterm elections, Hastert opted to leave leadership, before resigning from Congress in 2007. Hastert became a lobbyist and consultant after leaving office. In 2013, the FBI and IRS began investigating the former speaker surrounding suspicions that he was illegally structuring bank transactions. In 2015, Hastert was indicted for structuring bank transactions to evade reporting requirements and making false statements to the FBI. Hastert pleaded guilty in 2015 to violating banking laws by making repeated large cash withdrawals, which were revealed to be going to one of his victims. During the hearing, Hastert admitted to sexually abusing boys during his time as their wrestling coach. At his sentencing, U.S. District Judge Thomas M. Durkin called Hastert a "serial child molester," and sentenced him to 15 months in prison, a $250,000 fine and ordered him to participate in a sex offender program. Hastert was not charged with sex-related crimes, as the statutes of limitations had expired. He served 13 months in a federal prison before his release in 2017. Zachary Farden, the U.S. attorney for the Northern District of Illinois, said after Hastert was sentenced that there are "no winners in any of this" "Mr. Hastert's legend and legacy are gone, and in its place are a broken, humiliated man," Farden said. "That is how it should be." This article originally appeared on CBS News at https://www.cbsnews.com/news/dennis-hastert-dies-former-house-speaker-illinois/
