item.title: Soldiers and Gold Star families press Army leadership after deadly Iranian drone strike
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
WASHINGTON (AP) — On a sunny, cloudless morning on March 1, the day after President Donald Trump started the war against Iran , Chief Warrant Officer 3 Robert Marzan was coordinating critical Army supplies out of Port Shuaiba in Kuwait. In an instant, a drone crashed through the ceiling and exploded, killing Marzan, who had served in the military for 36 years. The force flung soldiers into the air, fragments of sheet metal and glass shards impaling them. The tin roof was peeled back "like opening up a sardine can," one soldier recalled. Six soldiers were killed and dozens were injured in the deadliest known strike on U.S. troops since Operation Epic Fury commenced on Feb. 28. For many, the attack at Port Shuaiba has receded into memory as the war nears its eighth month. But to those there that day and their families, it showed the cost of a hastily drawn conflict. The planning had apparent flaws, and commanders did not take intelligence reports of the Iranian threat seriously enough, leaving wounded soldiers questioning Army leadership and the military medical system. In the aftermath, many of the wounded — some with decades of service and combat experience — told The Associated Press that commanders had been warned that the facility, a rectangular building with wooden sides at a working seaport and industrial area south of Kuwait City, was particularly vulnerable to a drone strike. That warning went unheeded, the soldiers say. Some also said higher-ranking officers pushed for an all-clear to be called, but it's not certain from their accounts who ultimately made the decision to move soldiers out of a safer space in nearby bunkers. The wounded also would later say their serious injuries were not treated promptly or adequately in the weeks following the attack. "We have the right to know what really happened," Marzan's widow, Tina Marzan, told the AP. "If somebody messed up, those people need to be held responsible." In a chaotic battle, clarity is elusive Battlefield conditions are inherently chaotic and assessments drawn by those involved are often in tension. The AP's account of the attack is based on interviews with 13 soldiers, primarily officers, serving in key positions of responsibility there or familiar with high-level briefings leading up to the strike. Along with several Gold Star families — the military's designation for relatives of a soldier killed while on active duty — many are raising their concerns publicly for the first time and calling for the Army to reconcile what they say are failures of preparedness. Several soldiers spoke on the record, which is rare for troops still in the Army. Others spoke on the condition of anonymity for fear of reprisal. Some details of the attack have been reported by other news organizations, including The Washington Post and CBS News, but the AP is reporting other details for the first time. In the early days of the war, Trump described it as a "little excursion" that would end quickly but now has no off-ramp in sight. The toll can be measured in 19 U.S. personnel killed, more than 800 wounded and at least $44 billion spent to wage the fight. The Army declined to comment on the AP's reporting on the Port Shuaiba strike, saying it had not yet briefed the families of those killed on the outcome of its investigation into the attack. The Pentagon also declined to comment. "Out of respect for the primary next of kin who will be scheduled for briefs on the official findings of the completed investigation, we will not comment on specific details, individual accounts, or leaked portions of the report at this time," the Army said in a statement. The Army completed its investigation of the Port Shuaiba attack in June but has yet to release a report, citing the need to redact sensitive information, said an official familiar with the Army's investigation who spoke on the condition of anonymity because the report has not been released. Commanding officers followed a familiar playbook The story of the attack really begins in June 2025, when the U.S. bombed three nuclear sites in Iran . In anticipation of a counterstrike on U.S. troops in Kuwait, military planners relocated soldiers to Port Shuaiba, which the Army used for decades on the belief it was safer. In the lead-up to the war in February, that was the same playbook followed by Major Gen. John Hinson, the two-star general overseeing logistics for U.S. Central Command in the Middle East, and Brig. Gen. Clint Barnes, who led the 103rd Expeditionary Sustainment Command, an Iowa-based Army Reserve unit serving a nine-month deployment in Kuwait under Hinson's command. All six soldiers who died, and many of the dozens wounded, were from the 103rd. Hinson and Barnes chose not to deviate from the plan despite knowing that the port lacked defenses against drones and was seen as increasingly likely to be attacked, according to five officers and an enlisted soldier familiar with the U.S. intelligence and threat assessments. The generals were following orders made at U.S. Army Central, which oversees Army units in the Middle East, and Central Command to leave the nearby Army base, Camp Arifjan. Hinson declined to comment on the record for this story. Barnes did not respond to text messages and telephone calls. Even before the attack, the threat of a drone strike was well known. But the command team rejected proposals to move the entire logistics headquarters to other sites identified as safer locations outside Kuwait, farther away from Iran, according to Major Billy Key, an operations planner working for Barnes who has served in the Army for more than 20 years. Another officer confirmed the alternate plans were scuttled. The port was about 65 miles (104 kilometers) from the Iranian border. "Kuwait was just too close, that's the bottom line," Key said. "Kuwait was in striking distance of low-flying drones." Senior leadership believed that a core group of the more than 200 soldiers who had been handling logistics at Camp Arifjan needed to remain in Kuwait. Two senior officers, including Lt. Col. Tim Halbur, told the AP that there were communications advantages to being there, so a small crew of about 75 soldiers was sent to the port to set up a temporary field headquarters for logistics in the region. Dozens of troops from other units were also present. One enlisted soldier, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, said the command team is facing unfair criticism for hard decisions to balance its ability to carry out a crucial logistics mission with the inherent risks of war. But six officers told the AP that the logistics headquarters' jobs could have been done from a safer site outside Kuwait, so long as they had access to a secure communications network. "We did our work on a computer," Key told the AP. "We could have been anywhere." During meetings, officers overseeing protection told Hinson and Barnes, among others, that Port Shuaiba would not be safe for troops due to the lack of air protection against drones, according to five soldiers who were present: Key, Maj. Stephen Ramsbottom and three others familiar with high-level briefings who insisted on anonymity due to fear of reprisal. They said the generals were more focused on defending against missiles and were not prepared for drone warfare. "This type of fight has been going on for five years in Ukraine, and our excuse is we didn't expect it to happen to us," Ramsbottom said. "That's preposterous in my mind." While the three major U.S. military bases in Kuwait had bolstered air protection heading into the war, the only U.S. air support for Port Shuaiba came from a Patriot anti-missile system in the vicinity of Camp Arifjan that was ill-equipped for shooting down Iranian drones. While the system is capable of detecting the small aircraft, large numbers of drones are able to quickly deplete a battery, and the Patriot missiles cost vastly more than the drones. Using the system to down drones also then leaves the area vulnerable to far more deadly missile attacks. Neither Hinson nor Barnes was empowered to change anti-air or drone defenses at the site. "There was nothing that was going to intercept a threat coming at us other than ballistic missiles," Ramsbottom said. Just days before the relocation to the port in late February, a group of intelligence officers pressed Hinson and Barnes to not go there. Hinson asked whether Port Shuaiba was on a list of planned Iranian targets that had been obtained by U.S. intelligence before Operation Epic Fury and was told that it was not on the list but was considered a likely secondary target, according to two officers familiar with the meeting. The officers said Hinson still made the call to go. Lt. Gen. Patrick Frank, then leading Army Central, signed off on the plan to move to Port Shuaiba when Hinson briefed him, Halbur and another senior officer said. "Obviously, somewhere at the two-star, three-star level, they knew the intelligence reports," Halbur said. "We were just told, like, 'Hey, yeah, we'll be fine there.'" One officer who was involved in logistics and was wounded in the attack said staying at the Kuwaiti port seemed appropriate. Lt. Col. Arturo Lincón of the Defense Logistics Agency said Port Shuaiba had existing infrastructure for secure communications that could accommodate their unit and Jordan, where U.S. military operations also are based and many soldiers were being relocated, was already getting crowded. Captain was concerned about port's safety the morning of the attack At the start of the war, missiles from all sides lit up the screen inside the command post at the port. Soldiers rushed in and out of bunkers. They could feel booms shake the ground. That night, at least five quadcopter drones hovered over the port and appeared to be surveilling the U.S. military site, according to Key, who said one was only about 40 feet (12 meters) above him. He said he told senior officers what he saw, and it was passed up the chain. "That was the last I heard about it," he added. Intelligence briefings had warned that quadcopter drones were a sign of impending strikes. The next morning, March 1, Capt. Cody Khork, who oversaw safety for the unit and had strongly advised against going to the port, confided to Ramsbottom that he felt they should not leave their bunker because of the barrage of missiles and drones coming in, according to Ramsbottom. Both Khork and Ramsbottom were concerned that the radar being used to issue all-clears was not picking up low-flying drones. "We knew we were not safe," said Ramsbottom, who would end up with a piece of shrapnel sticking out of his head and a traumatic brain injury. "No one knew the drone situation." In the hours before the deadly strike, higher-ranking officers pushed Khork to get troops cleared to leave the bunkers, said Ramsbottom, who was with Khork in the bunker. The team was under tremendous pressure to carry out its mission, which included tracking munitions levels and fuel across the region, and that could not be done from inside the bunker. It remains unclear who ultimately made the decision to leave the bunkers, which were within several hundred feet of the operations center. Around 10 a.m., about 20 minutes after the final all-clear was issued, an Iranian drone smashed through the operation center's roof. Ramsbottom and Key recalled the drone struck seconds after Khork passed by them and said "good morning." Key was blasted into a metal cabinet and knocked unconscious. When he awoke, his ears were ringing and he stumbled through the rubble, coming across Khork's lifeless body. A group of soldiers helped take Khork's body from the wreckage to ensure he could be buried with dignity. Key later recounted the scene to Khork's parents at his funeral in Florida several weeks later, telling them their son appeared to die instantly. "I would have wanted someone to tell my family that if it were me," Key said. "I felt compelled to tell them exactly what happened." Lincón, a West Point graduate, remained conscious but was severely wounded by shrapnel and briefly lost his eyesight. Another wounded soldier bandaged him and got him out of the burning building. "Had it not been for those brave souls, there would have been a lot more, including myself, who probably (would have) burned there in place," Lincón said. Hinson and Barnes also suffered traumatic brain injuries from the blast, and Hinson's hand was hit with shrapnel. Planning was limited for a mass casualty event The soldiers based at Port Shuaiba headed into war without having implemented a broad-based plan for a mass casualty event, seven soldiers, including senior officers stationed there, told the AP. Soldiers who still had their phones intact used Google to locate the nearest medical facilities. Some among the wounded would later say their serious injuries were not treated promptly or adequately in the weeks after the strike. A medical service officer had prepared an evacuation plan that would have included setting up collection points for transporting wounded soldiers, but she was among the group sent to Jordan, and her plan was never briefed and put into place. She declined to comment. "I've been in Iraq and Afghanistan. I've been in combat operations before. I know what right looks like, and this was not right by any means," said Chief Warrant Officer 4 Jonathan Tenbrink, who has spent 35 years in the U.S. military and was wounded by shrapnel in his forehead, face, neck, shoulders and right arm. Relocating to Port Shuaiba, some soldiers acknowledged there was also a false sense of security. "It was the farthest thing from my mind that we would get hit there," said Lincón, who had deployed to Iraq and Afghanistan multiple times in his 27-year Army career. A hospital sent wounded soldiers to barracks rather than inpatient care Even for survivors, there was peril ahead. Halbur had been among a group of about nine soldiers medically evacuated, and he was having surgery at Walter Reed National Military Medical Center in Maryland within a week, describing his care there as "excellent." He said he was told by visiting top Army leadership that the Port Shuaiba soldiers were "the guinea pigs" for the medical system as Operation Epic Fury commenced. But other wounded soldiers, including those with serious head injuries and shrapnel wounds, had vastly different experiences of delayed care after the attack. One group, some of whom were treated at a Kuwaiti hospital for about 48 hours, holed up in residential homes in Kuwait for another week as Iran unleashed missiles and drones that made it risky for evacuation flights. Soldiers finally boarded a cargo plane flown to Germany. There, they say, they were not admitted to inpatient care at the military's main medical hub, the Landstuhl Regional Medical Center, but were sent to Army barracks because they had not been documented as combat-injured troops. About a week later they were placed into demobilization at Fort Hood in Texas, a process not focused on providing medical care. A Pentagon official told the AP that Landstuhl's mission is to stabilize patients to transfer them for specialized care at a military hospital in the U.S., rather than admit them. In a statement, the Pentagon said that all wounded troops who arrive at its medical facilities are evaluated and may be admitted based on the severity of the injury. Families of the fallen received a briefing In early July, Gold Star families received a briefing from Frank, who had just ended his rotation as head of Army Central Command, providing a broad overview of the investigation's findings. Tina Marzan said there was no admission of error. Frank did not say anything about Port Shuaiba's vulnerabilities, only that soldiers were moved around because attacks on other bases were expected, according to Marzan. Frank also told her that there was proper medical treatment available to those at Port Shuaiba, she said. "Whatever happened unfortunately does not bring my husband back," Marzan said. One senior officer filed a complaint against Barnes and Hinson to the Army's inspector general. But in a July 20 letter reviewed by the AP, the watchdog concluded that Barnes had not engaged in misconduct or "ignored reliable intelligence" in this complaint based on "the limited evidence" provided by the officer. The agency also noted this complaint against Hinson was withdrawn, which the officer disputed to the AP. The officer told the AP he relayed his conversations with Barnes discussing intelligence briefings but told investigators he had not directly interacted with Hinson. A wounded soldier can no longer salute Halbur, a father of two from Ankeny, Iowa, had been deployed as an Army reservist seven months earlier, hardly expecting to be on the front lines of a full-blown conflict. He had served for nearly 30 years, but today he can no longer salute. His dominant right arm will likely never be able to bend past 90 degrees again after the blast shattered his forearm in four places, including his elbow. "I can't squeeze both arms around my kids because my one arm won't allow me to do that anymore," Halbur said. "I want to coach my son's football team, but at the same time, I can't show them how to throw a football." He says that his children, age 7 and 8, are coming to learn that "dad's never going to be the same." He wears the names of the six soldiers who died at Port Shuaiba engraved in a metal wristband: Maj. Cody Khork, 35, an easygoing history buff; Master Sgt. Noah L. Tietjens, 42, a passionate martial arts instructor; Maj. Jeffrey R. O'Brien, 45, a father of three who loved playing the saxophone; Master Sgt. Nicole M. Amor, a 39-year-old mother of two with a knack for sarcasm; 20-year-old Sgt. Declan J. Coady, an avid outdoorsman and Eagle Scout; and Marzan, 54, a mentor to many younger soldiers. Khork, Tietjens, Amor and Coady received posthumous promotions. Halbur said that he looks at the wristband whenever he feels depressed by his arm's limitations. "I know that there are six families who would give that up in a heartbeat," he said. "So that always kind of gives me a little more motivation to not be so glum about the things that I can't do in my future. I'm still here." ___ Brook reported from New Orleans, Watson from San Diego and Bynum from Savannah, Ga. Associated Press journalists Nicholas Ingram in Ankeny, Iowa, and Thomas Peipert in Colorado Springs, Colo., contributed to this report. item.title: A common blood pressure drug shows promise for ADHD, animal studies suggest
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
(Dani Serrano/Moment RF/Getty Images) Experts say we need more options for treating ADHD , and a 2025 study suggests one option might already be stocked at the chemist. Around a quarter of patients with ADHD (attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder) find that existing medications for the condition do not improve their symptoms. And for others, the benefits of the stimulants commonly prescribed for ADHD are outweighed by the side effects: raised blood pressure, loss of appetite, headaches, trouble sleeping, and the risk of misuse. In a search for alternative treatments, a team of researchers from institutions across Europe has found a common blood pressure medication could be a good candidate: amlodipine, often sold under the brand name Norvasc. In an initial experiment, seven groups of spontaneously hypertensive rats ( which are sometimes used as a model of ADHD ) were each given a regimen of a different treatment and then faced with a regular test designed to assess their movement and level of spontaneity. The only drug that had a significant effect on rat behavior was amlodipine, administered daily for 30 days. ( CDC ) Having identified this potential candidate, the researchers proceeded to test on zebrafish, which were genetically modified to be more hyperactive and impulsive, behaviors we associate with ADHD in humans. When these fish were given amlodipine, however, their hyperactive traits effectively disappeared. In another set of experiments, researchers gave fish methylphenidate (better known by its brand name Ritalin) to see how it compared to amlodipine in terms of curbing impulsivity. Both medications had similarly significant effects when it came to reining in impulsive behaviors. While these animal studies suggest amlodipine could be worth researching further, we still don't know if it would actually be effective for treating ADHD in humans. Just because it seems to have some relevant effects on rats and genetically modified zebrafish doesn't mean it will work the same in humans with real ADHD. But these animal studies provide evidence for scientists to proceed to human clinical trials . The researchers did analyze existing UK Biobank data from people who happened to be taking amlodipine for hypertension, using genetic scores to estimate each person's ADHD risk. While this part of the study is observational (and therefore cannot show cause and effect), it reveals that people taking amlodipine were less likely to report mood swings or risk-taking, two traits linked to ADHD: another hint that this could be worth researching further. The good thing with amlodipine is that it's already approved for treating high blood pressure. In the US, more than 70 million people are taking this drug regularly, which means scientists are well aware of the risks and benefits. While it's generally considered safe, amlodipine comes with its own set of side effects: it can lead to fatigue, nausea, and gum irritation, to name a few. "Repurposing amlodipine, a well-established blood pressure medication, offers a promising and swift pathway to address ADHD symptoms," says neuroscientist Matthew Parker of the University of Surrey in the UK. "Our research indicates that, due to its existing approval and safety profile, amlodipine could be rapidly redeployed as a treatment option for ADHD, potentially providing relief to patients sooner than developing new medications." The research has been published in Neuropsychopharmacology . ScienceAlert stories are written, fact-checked, and edited by humans, never generated by AI. Don't miss a story, subscribe here. Two people killed after gunfire erupted at a neighborhood homecoming party in Georgia on Sunday have been identified. The shooting , which left another 35 injured, began at about 1:25 a.m. Sunday at a neighborhood party that spanned four blocks in the city of Vienna. Dooly County Sheriff Craig Peavy in a press conference described it as a “senseless act of violence” and said the investigation is ongoing. No arrests have been reported. The two victims killed have been named as Ja’Quavion Aderious Jackson, 21, and Macaleb Malik Jackson, 23. File image: Police tape is seen at the scene of a shooting. The 35 other victims ranged in age from 14 to 51, with their conditions ranging from stable to critical, Peavy said. The Georgia Bureau of Investigation has appealed to anyone with information about the shooting to contact authorities or submit an anonymous tip as law enforcement continues to investigate. Newsweek contacted the Georgia Bureau of Investigation for comment via email on Monday, outside of regular working hours. Authorities estimated that around 1,000 people had been at the party at the time of the shooting. “If you can imagine over 1,000 people, I would say, and they’re going every direction. item.title: As he exits Senate, Tillis sounds alarm on 'outsized influence' of executive branch
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
As Sen. Thom Tillis exits the Senate, he's blasting many of the advisers President Trump has surrounded himself with as "sycophants, and calling on his colleagues to stand up to executive power like the co-equal branch of government they are." The 66-year-old senior senator from North Carolina unloads on what he calls the "WTF moments" of the second Trump administration in a new book, "How to Lose Friends and Antagonize Presidents." Having served in the Senate during the Barack Obama, Joe Biden and both Trump presidencies, Tillis said he's increasingly worried about how the nation's system of checks and balances is being tested by the outsized influence of the executive branch. "We will have a sort of dictator king if we're not careful," he said. Make the Senate great again? Every recent White House has been eager to govern by executive order, something that's been especially true during the current Trump administration, Tillis said. Presidents, he said, fail to understand that Congress is a coequal branch that should be treated as a peer, and that Congress needs to act as such. "I would say the same thing for Democratic-controlled Senate under Biden and Obama," he said. "We always make the mistake when our guy's in office of conveying power to the White House. And I've had a real problem with that because it almost always comes back to bite you." He writes in his book of the risks of authoritarianism. Tillis said there's been "constant escalation" across four administrations of presidents ignoring Congress. "I want checks and balances. I want all three branches to have their individual role and continue to check power as they have for 250 years," he said. "I think because we've been such a successful democracy for so long, it's hard for the American people to understand how quickly we can lose it all." The Tillis tightrope act Tillis was first elected to the Senate in the 2014 midterm elections, just before the rise of Mr. Trump and his Make America Great Again populist movement took over the Republican Party. He said he's the same kind of conservative now that he was back then: "pro-Second Amendment, pro-life, limited government, fiscal restraint." "The only difference between me and a lotta people that call themselves true conservatives is I got a long list of things that were ratified and they don't," he said. The senator is now exiting Washington after a series of fights with the White House. The breaking point, he says, came in June 2025, after Tillis announced he would vote against Mr. Trump's One Big Beautiful Bill Act, arguing that it would push too many low-income North Carolinians off Medicaid. Mr. Trump responded by calling Tillis "a talker and complainer, not a doer," and threatening to back a primary challenger against Tillis. The senator decided he would retire instead of fighting for his seat. "I respect the president. I still feel like we have an odd relationship, where I've clearly made him angry," Tillis said recently. That was before details of his profanity-laced private texts with Trump about what prompted his retirement leaked, because Tillis included them as part of his upcoming book. Tillis said he is not done fighting, recently calling for Trump to fire Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. It should be noted that Tillis voted to confirm all of Mr. Trump's Cabinet nominees, including Hegseth. But he now calls that vote at the start of the second Trump administration his "biggest regret." While Tillis said he is glad "the president went in" to Iran, he thinks "they got so caught up after the immense success of the first strike that Hegseth probably didn't listen to his best military advice and say, 'Now we should probably move to a different posture.'" It's not the first time Tillis has gone after a member of Trump's cabinet. Last March at a senate hearing, he leveled a blistering critique of Department of Homeland Security Advisor Kristi Noem, calling out, among other things, the way she handled the deaths of Renee Good and Alex Pretti in Minneapolis. that went viral, Tillis ripped into Noem. "I was thinking about her calling people that were shot, potentially domestic terrorists," he said. "That's proven not to be true." Two days later, the president fired her. "I think Noem and Hegseth are probably the poster children for men and women who should never have the authority they've been granted," Tillis said. It's one example of the tightrope that Tillis has walked in the second Trump administration: saying how much he wants the president to succeed, while heaping blame on his advisers and subordinates. Besides Noem and Hegseth, Tillis s also highly critical of Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller, for "not looking around corners for" Mr. Trump. Tillis' balancing act in Washington also extends to the events of Jan. 6, 2021 . The senator is still angry about the attack on the Capitol, and threat to the peaceful transfer of power, calling what happened that day "despicable." Still, Tillis elected not to convict Mr. Trump after he left office during his second impeachment trial, criticizing the process as rushed and politicized. "Cheapening the impeachment process to prevent somebody from running in the future, I just don't buy it," he said. An "electoral bloodbath" in the midterms Asked if he fears a Jan. 6-like reaction if Trump-supported candidates lose their elections during the midterms, Tillis was somber. "I think there's a risk. I really do," he said, adding, "It would be another unforced error if we do that." Tillis predicts Republicans are about to suffer an "electoral bloodbath" in the upcoming midterm elections , with bread-and-butter affordability issues a main concern. Still, he said many of his colleagues are afraid to break with the White House. In his book, Tillis writes that at least 30 Republican senators have expressed reservations about many of Mr. Trump's actions, but usually are only willing to speak up privately, fearing that if the president decides to target them, their days will be numbered. "They don't want to bear the weight of the president. I get that. You're up for reelection? He'll target you in a primary. And so look, you know what all martyrs have in common? They're dead," Tillis said. "There were probably a few instances where if [you] kind of ripped the bandaid off early, then I think we'd have had a lot better midterm environment than we're confronted with now." item.title: Coast Guard suspends search for 6 medical jet passengers off Nantucket
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The U.S. Coast Guard on Sunday suspended the search for six people in a medical jet that went missing near Nantucket, Massachusetts, a day after debris from the plane was found. Search and rescue crews operated for approximately 66 hours to locate four Canadians and two Bermudian nationals on the plane that was traveling to Boston from Bermuda early Saturday morning, according to the U.S. Coast Guard. The Canadian-registered air ambulance jet had four crew members and two passengers aboard. Their next of kin have been notified, the Coast Guard said. Earlier, the Coast Guard confirmed that a debris field belonging to the missing Gulfstream G-100 was found Saturday night. The search for the missing passengers continued overnight off the coast of Nantucket, according to the Coast Guard's Northeast District , and spanned 4,445 miles before it was suspended. The Coast Guard outlined the extensive assets involved in the search, including an HC-144 Ocean Sentry airplane, an HC-130 Hercules airplane, an MH-60 Jayhawk helicopter, a 47-foot Motor Lifeboat and the FRC William Sparling, a Sentinel-class fast response cutter. "Suspending a search is not an easy decision," Rear Adm. Matthew Lake, Commander of the Northeast District, said in a statement. "We express our deepest condolences to the families and loved ones affected by the tragedy and our gratitude for our partner agencies who helped support search efforts." The plane took off from Bermuda's L.F. Wade International Airport at about 11:40 p.m. ET on Friday, according to data from FlightAware . It went missing after about 1 hour and 45 minutes in the air. FlightAware data show it quickly dropped from about 24,000 feet to 11,000 feet before losing contact. It had been set to land at Boston's Logan International Airport at about 1:30 a.m. local time. The Federal Aviation Administration confirmed it had lost contact with the plane around 1 a.m. local time Saturday and issued a Search and Rescue Alert Notice for the Gulfstream. Canada's foreign policy department said it was "deeply concerned by the disappearance" of the plane in a statement Sunday. "Our thoughts are with everyone on board and their loved ones," the statement said. "We thank the U.S. Coast Guard and all those involved in the search for their tireless efforts." Officials haven't been able to identify the aircraft components found among the debris, said Kastriot Kastrati, coordinator of the Coast Guard's search and rescue mission, at a briefing Sunday. "It's very difficult at this point to identify exactly what those components are," he said. "The debris that we have recovered, we've safeguarded and kept for future investigative efforts." The National Transportation Safety Board told CBS News on Sunday that it is monitoring the situation. "My thoughts are with everyone on board, as well as their families, loved ones and colleagues during this incredibly difficult time," Steve MacKinnon, Canada's minister of transport, said in a statement. item.title: Sailors are being offered up to $25,000 for risky oil runs through Hormuz
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
(Getty Images) Persian Gulf oil producers are paying as much as $40 million per tanker trip to keep crude flowing through the Strait of Hormuz as attacks on commercial vessels continue during the Iran war, The Wall Street Journal reported. Oil nevertheless is moving out of the Gulf at its fastest pace since the war began, according to the outlet. Producers increasingly are turning to journeys known as "shuttle runs," which allow customers to avoid sending their own tankers into the dangerous waterway. Under the system, very large crude carriers, or VLCCs, enter the Gulf through Hormuz, load crude at regional ports, and make the hazardous trip back through the strait. The oil is then transferred to another tanker waiting outside the Gulf for shipment to global markets, the Journal reported. Producers are paying between $30 million and $40 million for each round trip, or roughly $15 to $20 a barrel before insurance, according to shipbrokers cited in the report. "For many shipowners, the current market is generating revenues at levels rarely seen in the industry's recent history," Dimitris Maniatis, founder and CEO of maritime-risk company Marisks, told the Journal. Shipping crude directly from the Gulf has become even more expensive. The cost of hiring a supertanker to sail from the Persian Gulf to China topped $1.2 million a day in late September, up from about $231,400 before the war and less than $40,000 in early January, according to maritime data provider Clarksons Research. Sailors willing to enter the war zone are also commanding sharply higher pay, according to the Journal. Crew members, many from India, the Philippines, and China, are being offered two or three times their normal wages, while one Chinese staffing company has advertised bonuses of as much as $25,000 for a round trip. "Given the millions being made at the moment, that's absolutely nothing to the shipowners," Richard Matthews of shipbroker E.A. Gibson told the Journal. Demand for shuttle tankers reportedly surged after drone attacks shut Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline, prompting state-owned Aramco to join other Gulf producers using the system. Vortexa's Claire Jungman said the core shuttle fleet has grown from 30 vessels at the end of August to 39. The trade comes with potentially deadly consequences. U.K. Maritime Trade Operations said seven vessels have been struck since Sept. 28, while the International Maritime Organization and UKMTO reported nine commercial vessels attacked near Hormuz over the past two weeks, leaving two sailors injured and one dead. One first mate told the Journal his tanker crossed Hormuz twice in the past month at night with its lights off and windows shut. He said GPS signals disappeared for hours, forcing the crew to navigate using radar and surrounding landmarks. Even as Saudi Arabia gradually restores its East-West pipeline, analysts said they expect Hormuz to remain critical. "Saudi Arabia cannot find enough tankers if it wants to push three million barrels a day of crude exports from Yanbu up north to the Suez and then around Africa into markets in East Asia," Oil Brokerage's Anoop Singh told the Journal. Singh estimated that roughly two-thirds of Saudi oil flows ultimately will continue through Hormuz. © 2026 Newsmax. item.title: Christa Pike's lawyers warned her veins could make execution 'difficult and perhaps cruel'
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Christa Pike in court in Nashville in 2012. Photograph: Dipti Vaidya/USA TODAY NETWORK/Imagn Images/Reuters Connect A former lawyer for Christa Pike says he was not surprised that Tennessee botched its attempt to execute her because attorneys had warned that problems accessing her veins could make the procedure dangerous and potentially cruel. James Crowson, who represented Pike during part of her post-conviction appeals, said he had followed the case from afar before the failed execution at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville on 30 September. “Well, I can’t say I’m surprised,” said Crowson, who represented Pike while working for the Tennessee Post-Conviction Defender. “I knew that there were a number of defense filings saying that she had compromised veins, and that was going to be a difficult and perhaps cruel procedure for her because it was going to put her at risk for exactly what happened.” Pike, 50, on Sunday remained hospitalized and on a machine helping her breathe after Tennessee administered two doses of pentobarbital that failed to kill her, as far as an attorney now representing her knew, the lawyer said on the CNN program State of the Union. “She’s still in the hospital, on a ventilator, critically ill – we don’t really know the prognosis yet and may not know for several days,” Stephen Ferrell, an assistant federal defender, said to CNN host Jake Tapper. Ferrell told Tapper that he had not been able to personally see Pike, but “this is the extent of what we know”. Pike’s attorneys allege improperly placed intravenous lines allowed the drug with which she was injected to enter tissue rather than her bloodstream, leaving both arms severely injured. The Tennessee Department of Correction has maintained that it followed every step of the state’s lawful execution protocol. And the department said the protocol did not permit additional procedures after the steps carried out on Wednesday. Crowson said the accounts that officials followed the written protocol and that the execution was badly mishandled are not necessarily contradictory. “The state comes up with a protocol and, typically, states that are inclined to impose the death penalty don’t really include medicine or science in the discussions when they’re coming up with these protocols,” he said. Crowson said the reported injuries appeared consistent with the concerns raised before the execution, citing the theory that the drug entered surrounding tissue instead of circulating properly through Pike’s bloodstream. Pike was sentenced to death for the 1995 torture and killing of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, a fellow student at the Knoxville Job Corps. Pike was 18 at the time. Her then boyfriend and co-defendant, Tadaryl Shipp, was 17 and was ineligible for the death penalty. He received a sentence of life imprisonment. That gap in punishment based on a small age difference remains significant to Crowson. He said it illustrates what he views as the capricious nature of capital punishment. “She’s a few months older than the young man that was engaged in the same conduct, and she’s been fighting for her life now for 32 years,” Crowson said. “He’s still in prison, but hasn’t been subjected to the death penalty.” He said the age of 18 that was decisive for Pike “just seems like an arbitrary number”. Crowson represented Pike during a stage of her post-conviction case about 16 years earlier and said he visited her “dozens of times” on death row. He said he last spoke with her in 2009. He described Pike at the time as “very superficially charming” and attentive to people around her. But he said the person he knew bore little resemblance to the teenager whose crime sent her to death row. “I never saw the Christa that committed those crimes that put her in prison,” Crowson said. “That person exists, obviously.” The core of the post-conviction appeal, he said, was ineffective assistance of counsel. His team argued that Pike’s original attorneys failed to adequately present evidence about her mental illness, brain damage and history of severe childhood abuse during the sentencing phase. Pike ultimately exhausted her appeals without ever getting relief, despite her attorneys’ offering evidence of being diagnosed with bipolar and post-traumatic stress disorders. “It took me numerous years to even realize the gravity of what I’d done,” Pike had said in an earlier petition for clemency. “Even more to accept how many lives I affected. I took the life of someone’s child, sister, friend. It sickens me now to think I had the ability to commit such a crime.” Crowson more recently said “there was a lot that was left out” at the time of Pike’s conviction. “Would it have made a difference? I don’t know. There are a lot of people who feel very strongly, and her crime was grisly and horrifying.” What happens next depends on whether Pike ultimately survives the botched execution – and, if she does, the extent of any lasting injuries. Crowson said he expects intense pressure on Bill Lee, Tennessee’s governor, to commute Pike’s sentence to life imprisonment if she recovers. If she suffered serious neurological damage, he said, questions about her competency would become central to any attempt by Tennessee to execute her again. The fallout of the botched execution widened on Saturday when Lee announced that Frank Strada, the Tennessee Department of Correction commissioner, would resign later in October. Lee has ordered an independent review and halted executions in the state for the remainder of the year. Strada’s resignation was a predictable consequence of a botched execution now under national scrutiny, according to Crowson, who said: “Whenever you have a disaster like this, there’s going to be some fallout.” Furthermore, Pike’s was at least the fifth execution Strada had botched since 2022 in Tennessee as well as Arizona, where he previously worked, according to death penalty lawyers. Crowson said he hopes that Pike’s case results in the government taking a closer look at the death penalty as a functional legal punishment. He said there is a clear pattern between people who are sentenced to death and their history of trauma and mental illness not being accounted for during trial and sentencing. “I think we as a nation have a strange relationship with mental illness,” he said. “It’s just so often discounted and mocked. It’s unfortunate.” This article originally appeared on The Guardian at https://www.yahoo.com/news/us/articles/christa-pike-lawyers-had-warned-110055419.html
